title: The nikah ceremony
hookLine: a sermon, an offer and an acceptance, witnesses, and a blessing passed around the room

lines: A MOSQUE, A LIVING ROOM, A HALL.
A LINE GOES AROUND THE ROOM.
cards: The room might be a mosque, a living room, or a rented hall with too many folding chairs. The clothes change from country to country; the food changes even more.
But underneath all of it, the nikah itself is short, and its main pieces are few. A brief sermon. An offer, and an acceptance.
Witnesses who hear it. And then a short line goes around the room, said again and again to the couple, by aunts, friends and strangers.

teach.h: A SERMON: FROM A SINGLE SOUL.

teach.b: Tradition opens the nikah with a short sermon the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught, reported in Sunan Abu Dawud: praise of God, and verses of the Qur'an about mindfulness of God and speaking straight.
One of them, from surah al-Nisa, reminds everyone that all people were created from a single soul, and its mate from it. A wedding begins by remembering where every couple comes from.

teach.h: IJAB AND QABUL, AND THE MAHR.
teach.b: Second, the offer and the acceptance: in Arabic, ijab and qabul. One side offers, the other accepts, in clear words. It's a contract, an 'aqd.
And the Qur'an asks that the bride receive a gift, the mahr. In Pickthall's translation: "And give unto the women (whom ye marry) free gift of their marriage portions." The gift is hers.
Third, the witnesses. A nikah isn't a secret. The schools of law set out the conditions, the witnesses and the role of the bride's guardian, and they differ on the details.
But the shape is public: people hear it, and can say they heard it. Fourth, the blessing.
In Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, when the Prophet congratulated someone on a marriage, he would say, in paraphrase: may Allah bless you, and send blessing upon you, and bring you together in goodness.
At weddings you may hear a short form of it: barakallahu lakuma, may Allah bless you both. Lakuma means you two. The blessing is spoken to the pair, together.

how: A Muslim marriage is a contract (nikah) made by offer and acceptance before witnesses, with a mahr for the bride, often opened by a short sermon; guests may congratulate the couple with "barakallahu lakuma".

games.q: you're a guest at a nikah. the offer has been made and accepted, and people are lining up to greet the couple. what do they say?
games.why: barakallahu lakuma, may Allah bless you both: a short form of the blessing the Prophet gave at marriages.

practice: Say it slowly, a piece at a time: barakallahu, lakuma, barakallahu lakuma, may Allah bless you both. Bring to mind a couple, newly married or married for decades, and if you pray, hold them in mind as you say it.
If you don't, just learn the sound of it, so the next time you hear it at a wedding, you'll know it's a blessing being passed around the room.

wordCard.voice: The nikah ceremony. A sermon, an offer and an acceptance, a gift for the bride, witnesses, and a blessing for the two of them. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: barakallahu lakuma. A blessing for two, said by everyone in the room. Go gently, and see you next time.
